opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of my favorite things to argue about, because triangle layers are both the most elegant and the most annoying part of the AlphaFold-style architectures.

The core idea is that you keep a pair representation, an L-by-L grid of embeddings for every pair of residues, and you update each edge using the other two edges of every triangle it's part of. So if I want to refine my belief about residues i and j, I look at all the k's and ask what i–k and k–j imply. That's basically a soft way of enforcing geometric consistency. If i is close to k and k is close to j, that constrains how far i can be from j. You're baking something like the triangle inequality into the network's inductive bias, and empirically it matters a lot. When people ablate it, structure quality drops noticeably, especially for long-range contacts.

The catch is cost. Triangle multiplication and triangle attention are cubic in sequence length. For a few hundred residues that's fine. When you get into big complexes, antibody-antigen systems, or multi-chain assemblies with thousands of tokens, memory and compute blow up. A huge amount of engineering effort, like chunking, custom kernels, and low-precision tricks, goes into just making those layers fit on a GPU.

So the tradeoffs I think about are roughly these.

**Expressivity versus scaling.** Triangle updates give you a strong prior that's really sample-efficient. You don't need to learn geometric consistency from scratch. But as you scale data and parameters, you start wondering whether a plain transformer with enough capacity would just learn that structure itself, the way we've seen in other domains where hand-designed inductive biases eventually get washed out by scale.

**Where you spend your depth.** Do you keep a heavy pair stack, or move more of the work into the single representation and the structure or diffusion module? The newer generative architectures have trended toward lighter trunks and putting more of the burden on the diffusion side, partly for exactly this reason.

**Multiplication versus attention.** In my experience, triangle multiplicative updates do a lot of the heavy lifting relative to their cost, and triangle attention is more expensive for a smaller marginal gain. So if you're budget-constrained, that's often the first place to trim.

**Generation versus prediction.** For pure structure prediction, the consistency prior is great. For design or generative tasks, where you're sampling many candidates or working at large scale, the cubic cost hurts more and you might accept a slightly weaker prior for much higher throughput.

My overall take is that triangle layers are a really good bias for the data regime we're in, since protein structure data is still pretty limited compared to text or images. I wouldn't bet on them being permanent, though. I think we'll see either sparser or approximate versions that keep most of the geometric benefit at sub-cubic cost, or models that are big enough and trained on enough data, including synthetic or distilled structures, that they can get away with something simpler. The interesting research question is figuring out exactly which part of the triangle update is doing the work, so you can keep that and drop the rest.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've spent a lot of time thinking about, because triangle attention and triangle multiplication are kind of the signature move of AlphaFold 2, and they're also the thing everyone complains about when they try to scale these models.

The basic intuition is that if you want to predict a structure, pairwise representations are the natural object. You've got a residue-by-residue grid, and each cell is encoding something like "how do i and j relate." The problem is that geometry isn't just pairwise. If I know the distance from A to B and from B to C, that constrains A to C. The triangle inequality is the simplest version of that, and the triangle layers are basically a way to let the network reason about those three-body consistency constraints directly in the pair representation. Each pair ij gets updated by looking at all the k's, so you're routing information through third residues. That inductive bias turned out to be really powerful. It's a big part of why AlphaFold 2 got the geometry so right rather than just producing contact maps that looked plausible but weren't physically realizable.

The cost is the part that hurts. You're doing an operation that's cubic in sequence length, and you're doing it in a pair representation that's already quadratic in memory. So for a 300-residue protein that's fine, for a 1,500-residue complex you're suddenly in a regime where a single forward pass is eating up a whole accelerator, and training on long inputs becomes this cropping-and-sampling game. And then if you want to move to things like whole antibody-antigen complexes, or nucleic acids, or multi-chain assemblies, the length just keeps growing.

So the tradeoff question is: how much of that cubic compute is actually buying you accuracy, and how much is just the architecture we inherited? My honest take is that it's somewhere in between. There's pretty good evidence now that you can get a lot of the benefit with cheaper approximations. You can do triangle multiplication but skip triangle attention, which is the more expensive of the two, and lose less than you'd expect. You can do the triangle updates less frequently, or only in a subset of blocks. And a lot of the recent work, including stuff coming out around AlphaFold 3 and the various open reproductions, has been quietly trimming these layers while keeping the core idea of a pair representation that reasons about geometry.

The other axis is whether you need the pair representation to be the main thing at all. There's a whole direction, and this is where I'd put a lot of the protein language model work and the structure-token approaches, where you push more capacity into a sequence-level representation and treat the pair stuff as lightweight. Those models are dramatically cheaper and scale beautifully with data, but when you look at hard cases, like multimers, or things with very few homologs, or anything where you need precise interface geometry, the explicit pair reasoning still tends to win. So I don't think triangle layers are going away. I think they're becoming a tool you reach for selectively rather than the backbone of the whole network.

The way I'd summarize it is: triangle layers are an extremely good inductive bias for a data-poor regime. We had, what, a couple hundred thousand structures in the PDB. When you don't have a lot of data, you want the architecture to do the work. As data and compute grow, you can afford to relax some of those priors and let the model learn geometry consistency on its own. We're kind of in the middle of that transition right now, and the interesting engineering is figuring out exactly which parts you can relax and which parts you really can't.

astra-6.text:
I think the key tradeoff is the geometric structure you get versus the computational cost. If you’re maintaining a representation for every pair of residues, a triangle layer lets the relationship between i and j depend on a third residue, k. That’s a useful inductive bias for a protein: those relationships shouldn’t be independent of one another.

But the pair representation already has quadratic memory cost, and aggregating over that third residue introduces cubic compute in the straightforward implementation. As you move to longer sequences or larger complexes, that becomes expensive.

So I’d ask where you actually need that geometric reasoning. Do you need triangle operations in every block, or can you use cheaper updates for most of the network and spend that compute in a few places? And you have to measure actual runtime and memory, because the implementation matters a lot. It’s a strong architectural prior, but whether it’s worth it depends on the task, the sequence lengths, and what else you could do with the same compute.

I think the main tradeoff is how much geometric structure you build into the model versus how much computation you spend on it. If you maintain a representation for every pair of residues, a triangle layer lets you update the relationship between i and j using a third residue, k. That’s a useful inductive bias: those relationships shouldn’t be independent if they’re describing the same three-dimensional structure.

The downside is the cost. You’re already carrying a quadratic pair representation, and the triangle operations can introduce cubic compute in sequence length. So as you move to longer proteins or larger complexes, that becomes a pretty substantial bottleneck.

The question I’d ask is whether you need that operation everywhere. Can you use fewer triangle layers, or put them at particular stages where geometric consistency matters most? Removing them might make each step cheaper, but if the model then needs more data or more training to learn the same relationships, it’s not necessarily a win. I’d look at the accuracy you get for the total compute budget, especially as sequence length increases.
